title: Technical Product Management

resources.title: Learning user needs
resources.notes: Inspected researching, writing and validating needs. Treat opinions without user evidence as assumptions; government-service examples are contextual.

resources.title: How discovery works
resources.notes: Inspected problem definition, constraints and proceed/stop decisions. No public service, account or research participant is required for the original synthetic assignments.

resources.title: Informed consent for research
resources.notes: Inspected consent, withdrawal and research-data handling. Use hypothetical protocols; optional real participation needs actual informed consent and appropriate privacy safeguards.

resources.title: Writing user stories and acceptance criteria
resources.notes: Inspected actor/need/goal, acceptance criteria and supporting evidence links. A story is not a substitute for a complete implementation contract.

resources.title: Developing an outcome-oriented roadmap
resources.notes: Inspected vision, iteration, collaboration and roadmap-versus-backlog distinctions. Public-sector cadence examples are not mandatory deadlines for learners.

resources.title: Set meaningful performance metrics
resources.notes: Inspected purpose, benefits, hypotheses, definitions and data sources. UK government mandatory KPI publication is not a requirement for these private synthetic exercises.

resources.title: Moderated usability testing
resources.notes: Inspected neutral task design, discussion guides and observation. A labelled self-walkthrough cannot establish independent customer behavior.

resources.title: Choosing technology deliberately
resources.notes: Inspected reversibility, total cost, data control and contextual decisions. No cloud provisioning, paid service or procurement is assigned.

resources.title: Diagnosing sample ratio mismatch
resources.notes: Inspected SRM causes across assignment, execution, logging and analysis. Historical platform examples are not current universal incidence estimates or proof about a learner's experiment.

resources.title: Principles of Managerial Accounting: break-even analysis
resources.license: Publisher edition terms; official link only
resources.notes: Inspected CVP assumptions, contribution margin and break-even units/revenue. Assignments use original numerical cases; no book, illustrations or answer bank is rehosted.

resources.title: Canarying releases
resources.notes: Inspected release engineering principles and balancing release velocity/reliability. Operational canary health checks do not automatically constitute randomized product-impact experiments.

resources.title: Metrics and instruments
resources.notes: Inspected runtime metric events, instrument types and aggregation. Local output is sufficient; there is no requirement to purchase a telemetry backend or send learner data to one.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Frame a bounded problem, distinguish evidence from assumptions and connect a synthetic user journey to technical constraints and meaningful outcomes.
stageOutcomes.evidence: An ethical discovery protocol, original segments/jobs, a system map and metric definitions with explicit populations and denominators; no invented research participants.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Translate a hypothetical need into a traceable PRD, dependency-aware priorities, reproducible instrumentation and a neutral research/experiment design.
stageOutcomes.evidence: A requirement-to-test matrix, a sensitivity-aware roadmap, executable local funnel analysis and a labelled self-walkthrough or genuinely consented research record.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Make defensible platform, experiment, unit-economics and risk decisions while checking validity, uncertainty, operational constraints and ownership.
stageOutcomes.evidence: An API/build-buy decision, an SRM and contamination audit, unit-labelled financial calculations and a risk/sequencing decision that can reject an attractive but unsupported release.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Defend a launch/defer decision, resolve stakeholder trade-offs and revise a roadmap from reproducible evidence without manufacturing impact claims.
stageOutcomes.evidence: An integrated three-project case-study dossier separating real implemented behavior, hypothetical personas/experiments, local measurements and independently demonstrated learner work.

modules.title: 01. Problems, research ethics and segments
modules.description: Establish what is known, assumed and ethically researchable before committing to a feature.

lessons.title: Frame a problem without inventing user evidence
objectives: Separate a user need, proposed solution, assumption and observed fact.
Design an ethical discovery protocol with a bounded stop/proceed decision.

topics.title: Evidence before solutions
details: A stakeholder request is evidence that the request was made, not proof that all users need the proposed feature.
Label facts, hypotheses and unknowns explicitly; a synthetic persona is a learning device, not a research participant.

topics.title: Ethical discovery
details: A research protocol names purpose, voluntary participation, data minimization, retention and withdrawal.
The required path uses a hypothetical protocol and synthetic data. Real interviews remain optional and must not be fabricated.

reading.locator: Define the problem and What to find out in discovery: reframe a proposed solution, identify constraints and choose what evidence would justify proceeding.

assignment.title: A synthetic recovery-discovery brief
instructions: Use the fictional request 'operators need a retry button for a failed batch' and write three competing explanations for the problem.
Create a fact/assumption/unknown table; label every invented operator and event as synthetic rather than claiming interviews.
Write a hypothetical consent/data-retention protocol and a discovery question that could justify not building the button.
deliverables: A problem brief with an evidence-status table.
A hypothetical ethical research protocol and stop/proceed criteria.
acceptanceCriteria: The problem is distinct from the retry-button solution.
No fictional interview, customer adoption or observed pain is presented as a fact.
The protocol includes voluntary participation, minimal data, withdrawal and a decision that could reject the feature.

questions.prompt: A stakeholder says every operator needs a retry button, but no operator evidence exists. How should the claim be recorded?
choices: An assumption to investigate
A validated user need
An observed adoption result
questions.answer: An assumption to investigate
questions.explanation: A request establishes stakeholder preference, not the population's actual need. Discovery must distinguish that assumption from directly observed user evidence.

questions.prompt: Explain one reason discovery might reject the retry button even if users report failed batches.
questions.answer: The underlying need may be reliable recovery, while a retry button could duplicate unsafe effects or hide a contract defect. Investigate root causes and alternatives before choosing the interface.
questions.explanation: A well-framed need allows several solutions and a no-build decision. Reports of failure do not establish that replay is safe or that a button addresses the root cause.

reviewPrompts: Which sentence in your brief is least supported?
What observation could change your proposed decision?

lessons.title: Describe segments and jobs as testable hypotheses
objectives: Distinguish a behavior-based segment from an invented demographic stereotype.
Write a job with context, desired progress and a plausible competing approach.

topics.title: Segmentation
details: Segment by relevant behavior, constraints and decision context rather than unnecessary sensitive attributes.
A segment hypothesis needs disconfirming evidence; one persona cannot stand in for a population.

topics.title: Jobs and alternatives
details: A job describes desired progress in a situation, not a mandated screen or technology.
Current workarounds and choosing not to act are credible alternatives that affect priority.

reading.locator: Understanding, writing and validating user needs; retain the context and goal while treating non-user opinions and invented personas as assumptions.

assignment.title: Three original retrieval-use situations
instructions: Invent three explicitly hypothetical situations for searching permitted operating guidance: routine lookup, ambiguous incident and revoked guidance.
For each, name the context, desired progress, existing workaround and relevant access constraint without using protected demographic categories.
Propose one observation that would disconfirm each segment and show how it changes your initial priority.
deliverables: A three-segment/job/alternative matrix.
A disconfirmation and prioritization note.
acceptanceCriteria: Every segment is labelled hypothetical and based on relevant behavior or constraints.
Jobs describe desired outcomes rather than demanding a specific search feature.
Each segment has a plausible alternative and a disconfirming observation.

questions.prompt: Which segment is most useful for the bounded retrieval case?
choices: Everyone aged 25 to 35
Operators resolving an ambiguous incident with restricted guidance access
All people who like modern technology
questions.answer: Operators resolving an ambiguous incident with restricted guidance access
questions.explanation: The incident context and access constraint explain meaningful product behavior. Age and vague technology preferences do not establish the relevant job or a need for sensitive profiling.

questions.prompt: Rewrite 'users want an AI chatbot' as a job hypothesis with an alternative.
questions.answer: During an unfamiliar incident, an operator wants to identify current permitted guidance quickly enough to choose a safe next action; asking a colleague or using a document index may be alternatives.
questions.explanation: The reformulation separates desired progress from a chosen interface and leaves room to compare simpler solutions against the same outcome.

reviewPrompts: Which attribute in your segment actually changes the product decision?
What evidence would make your preferred segment less important?

modules.title: 02. Technical journeys and outcome definitions
modules.description: Connect user-facing needs to system boundaries and metrics whose populations and units are explicit.

lessons.title: Map a journey across technical and responsibility boundaries
objectives: Trace a product journey through application, data and external-effect boundaries.
Separate implemented behavior, a learning target and an untested integration.

topics.title: System literacy
details: A successful HTTP response, a database commit and an external effect are different events.
Identify ownership, durable state, retries and failure visibility before proposing a user-facing promise.

topics.title: Honest scope
details: A local simulated provider is not real payment processing or distributed availability.
A reference implementation demonstrates only its reviewed scope; its existence is not independent learner competence.

reading.locator: Understand the landscape, start with prototypes and allow for evolution. Identify existing dependencies, data control and which assumptions a prototype can actually test.

assignment.title: A commerce journey and boundary map
instructions: Map submit order, reserve stock, persist intent, simulated provider effect and reconcile outcome using the original commerce learning brief.
Identify which steps share a transaction and which belong to another persistent component; explicitly distinguish a SQLite reference from PostgreSQL-specific learning.
Mark each claim implemented, learner extension or unknown, then write a user-visible response for one uncertain provider outcome.
deliverables: A journey/data/responsibility diagram.
A scoped capability table and uncertain-outcome response contract.
acceptanceCriteria: The map distinguishes request success, durable intent and provider effect.
Local/synthetic and stack-specific limits remain explicit.
Unknown outcomes are communicated honestly instead of being called completed orders.

questions.prompt: An order is stored but its simulated provider outcome is unknown. Which product response is defensible?
choices: Payment definitely succeeded
The entire distributed workflow is exactly once
Order accepted; provider outcome is pending reconciliation
questions.answer: Order accepted; provider outcome is pending reconciliation
questions.explanation: Durable acceptance does not prove an external effect. A pending reconciliation state communicates the known boundary without inventing success or an exactly-once guarantee.

questions.prompt: Why is a diagram that places a separate provider database inside the order transaction misleading?
questions.answer: It implies atomic rollback across components that do not share that transaction. The design needs an explicit retry, idempotency and reconciliation/compensation policy for the separate effect.
questions.explanation: A diagram is part of the product contract. Drawing a false atomic boundary can lead stakeholders to promise outcomes the implementation cannot guarantee.

reviewPrompts: Where can this journey be durable but incomplete?
Which promise would require a different implementation?

lessons.title: Define outcomes, inputs and guardrails with correct denominators
objectives: Distinguish activity metrics from user outcomes and safety guardrails.
Specify population, grain, numerator, denominator, window and undefined behavior.

topics.title: Metric meaning
details: A click or request count measures activity, not necessarily a successful user outcome.
Define the eligible population before measuring completion; denominator changes can create artificial improvements.

topics.title: Numeric communication
details: A fraction, percent and percentage-point difference are distinct quantities.
An empty eligible population produces an undefined rate, not automatically zero or perfect success.

reading.locator: Base metrics on service purpose, define benefits, develop hypotheses and decide what to measure; document data sources and population boundaries.

assignment.title: An auditable recovery-success metric
instructions: Define successful recovery for a fictional cohort of 80 eligible failed runs, of which 20 meet the declared completion checks.
Specify one input metric, one outcome metric and one correctness guardrail with windows, exclusions and grain.
Compute the completion fraction and percent, then show what the report should display when no runs are eligible.
deliverables: A metric dictionary with populations and units.
A hand-calculated rate table including the empty-population case.
acceptanceCriteria: The outcome rate is 0.25 as a fraction and 25 as a percent number.
Each metric states its population, grain, numerator/denominator and window.
The zero-denominator case is explicitly undefined rather than a fabricated success rate.

questions.prompt: Which metric best measures the declared recovery outcome rather than interface activity?
choices: Eligible failed runs restored with reconciled outputs divided by eligible failed runs
Number of clicks on Retry
Number of visits to the recovery page
questions.answer: Eligible failed runs restored with reconciled outputs divided by eligible failed runs
questions.explanation: The numerator checks the intended result and the denominator identifies the eligible population. Clicks and visits can rise while recovery remains incorrect.

questions.prompt: 20 of 80 eligible runs meet all recovery checks. Enter the success percentage as a number, not a fraction.
questions.explanation: Twenty is one quarter of eighty. The fraction is 0.25, so the requested percentage number is 25; entering 0.25 would use the wrong unit.

questions.prompt: Explain why removing failed runs from the denominator makes a recovery metric misleading.
questions.answer: Eligibility would depend on the outcome, excluding precisely the failures the metric should represent. Define inclusion before observing success and retain failures in the cohort.
questions.explanation: Outcome-dependent selection can mechanically improve a rate without improving the system or the user journey.

reviewPrompts: Who is excluded from your denominator, and why?
Is a better activity metric necessarily a better outcome?

modules.title: 03. PRDs, acceptance and uncertain priorities
modules.description: Specify a bounded product change and choose work using dependencies and evidence rather than feature volume.

lessons.title: Write a PRD that traces needs to observable behavior
objectives: Write a concise PRD with scope, non-goals, constraints and acceptance checks.
Trace a requirement to code/test evidence without assuming a reference implements it.

topics.title: Requirement quality
details: A requirement states an observable outcome or constraint, not merely a technology choice.
Include denied, empty, duplicate and failure paths rather than describing only the happy path.

topics.title: Traceability
details: A requirement, its implementation and its test are different artifacts linked by evidence.
An unimplemented requirement remains proposed; passing an unrelated test does not close it.

reading.locator: How to write a user story, Acceptance criteria and Planning with your user stories; link each desired outcome to supporting evidence.

assignment.title: A bounded permission-aware lookup PRD
instructions: Write a short PRD for a synthetic user who needs current permitted guidance, including non-goals such as generated answers if they are not implemented.
Specify acceptance for allowed access, cross-tenant denial, missing evidence and a withdrawn document.
Create a requirement-to-implementation-to-test table, using explicit proposed or unknown labels where no verified implementation exists.
deliverables: A bounded PRD with failure and authorization criteria.
A traceability matrix separating implemented, proposed and unknown items.
acceptanceCriteria: Every requirement has an observable acceptance check.
Non-goals and privacy/access boundaries are explicit.
No missing implementation or unrelated passing test is represented as verified requirement coverage.

questions.prompt: A PRD says 'the search is fast and safe.' What is the most useful next change?
choices: Add more technology names
Define a bounded latency workload and explicit denied-access cases
Mark it done because the homepage loads
questions.answer: Define a bounded latency workload and explicit denied-access cases
questions.explanation: Observable workload and boundary checks make the requirement testable. Technology labels or a loading homepage do not establish performance or authorization behavior.

questions.prompt: What should the traceability row say when a desired revocation control is not implemented?
questions.answer: Proposed or not implemented, with the missing behavior, owner and acceptance evidence needed to close it; do not substitute a link to an unrelated test.
questions.explanation: Traceability should reveal gaps rather than hide them. A learning brief can contain a target that the supplied reference does not yet cover.

reviewPrompts: Which acceptance check covers a denied request?
Which row is still proposed and what would close it?

lessons.title: Prioritize with uncertainty, dependencies and opportunity cost
objectives: Compare feasible work without treating a prioritization score as objective truth.
Explain how uncertainty and dependencies can reverse an apparent ranking.

topics.title: Prioritization inputs
details: Reach, impact, confidence and effort must have stated meanings and comparable units.
Scores reflect assumptions; a confident-looking number does not validate demand or override safety prerequisites.

topics.title: Roadmaps
details: A roadmap describes intended outcomes and sequencing, not a promise to complete every backlog item.
Prerequisites, operational risks and the option to defer constrain the feasible sequence.

reading.locator: Roadmap principles: take iterations toward a vision, express value and objectives, distinguish roadmaps from backlogs, and revise collaboratively as evidence changes.

assignment.title: A priority decision that can change
instructions: Compare three original hypothetical improvements: safer retry, lineage preview and a cosmetic dashboard; state assumed reach, impact, confidence and effort.
For one option use assumed reach 120, impact 2, confidence 0.5 and effort 4; compute reach times impact times confidence divided by effort, then vary confidence.
Draw dependencies and explain why a lower-scoring safety prerequisite or deferral may come before the numerically highest option.
deliverables: A unit-labelled priority/sensitivity table.
An outcome roadmap with dependencies and a rejected alternative.
acceptanceCriteria: The stated example score is 30 and all inputs are labelled hypothetical.
Changing assumptions is shown to affect the decision instead of presenting a score as validated demand.
The sequence respects dependencies and records opportunity cost and a credible defer option.

questions.prompt: A feature has the highest assumed priority score but depends on an unimplemented safety control. What follows?
choices: Skip the safety control
The score proves users demand immediate release
Evaluate the prerequisite and feasible sequence before committing
questions.answer: Evaluate the prerequisite and feasible sequence before committing
questions.explanation: A scoring heuristic ranks assumptions, not executable plans. Dependencies and safety constraints determine whether an option is feasible and acceptable.

questions.prompt: Using reach 120, impact 2, confidence 0.5 and effort 4, enter reach times impact times confidence divided by effort.
questions.explanation: The weighted impact is 120 times 2 times 0.5, which is 120; dividing by effort 4 gives 30. This is an assumed planning score, not measured value.

questions.prompt: Explain why changing effort from days to hours in only one row invalidates a score comparison.
questions.answer: The denominators no longer share units, so one option's score changes due to representation rather than economics or difficulty. Normalize effort units before comparing.
questions.explanation: A ratio can be numerically computed with inconsistent units while becoming meaningless as a ranking device.

reviewPrompts: Which assumption most changes the selected option?
What are you choosing not to do?

modules.title: 04. Instrumentation, usability and experimental design
modules.description: Produce reproducible measurement and research plans without confusing synthetic examples with real participants.

lessons.title: Implement a funnel with explicit event and cohort contracts
objectives: Define event identity, grain and eligibility before calculating a funnel.
Detect duplicate, orphan and missing events using a runnable local analysis.

topics.title: Event contracts
details: An event needs identity, occurrence/ingestion time, version and a documented actor/session grain.
Collect only synthetic identifiers and necessary fields; do not add analytics to the learning tracker or send private data to a service.

topics.title: Funnels
details: A completion event without a valid eligible start cannot automatically join the start cohort.
Deduplication, ordering and windows change the denominator and require independently checked examples.

reading.locator: Find data sources and decide what to measure; connect the service hypothesis to clearly defined measurements and validate what the data can answer.

assignment.title: A local five-event funnel
instructions: Create five original synthetic events: actor A start twice with the same event ID, A finish, B start and C finish without a start.
Write a local SQL query or Python analysis that deduplicates event IDs and restricts completion to the eligible starting cohort.
Extend the fixture with out-of-order ingestion and an event outside the declared window; retain the hand-calculated cohort and query output.
deliverables: A versioned synthetic event contract and executable local analysis.
Golden cohort results and duplicate/orphan/window regression cases.
acceptanceCriteria: The base cohort has two distinct starters and one eligible finisher, giving 50 percent conversion.
The duplicate start and orphan finish do not inflate counts.
The window, event-time/ingestion-time rule and synthetic data boundary are explicit.

questions.prompt: Actor C has a finish event but no eligible start. Under the declared starting-cohort funnel, how is C handled?
choices: Excluded from that completion numerator and investigated as an orphan
Counted as a successful starter
Used to infer a missing start without disclosure
questions.answer: Excluded from that completion numerator and investigated as an orphan
questions.explanation: The cohort was defined by eligible starts. Adding an inferred start would change the data and denominator; the orphan remains visible for instrumentation diagnosis.

questions.prompt: After deduplication the declared cohort has two starters and one eligible finisher. Enter conversion as a percentage number.
questions.explanation: One eligible completion among two starters is a fraction of 0.5, or 50 percent. Counting duplicate starts or orphan completions would use a different, invalid cohort.

questions.prompt: Why can an ingestion timestamp be inappropriate for ordering a user journey?
questions.answer: Events may arrive late or out of order. Define occurrence-time and eligibility/window rules, preserve ingestion time for diagnostics, and test delayed arrivals rather than assuming arrival order is journey order.
questions.explanation: Instrumentation transport behavior is not the same as user behavior. Mixing the clocks can reorder steps or exclude valid events without explanation.

reviewPrompts: Which malformed event would most distort this funnel?
Can another learner reproduce your numerator from raw events?

lessons.title: Design neutral usability tasks and falsifiable experiments
objectives: Write a usability protocol that does not reveal the intended answer.
Define a falsifiable hypothesis, comparison, assignment unit and guardrails.

topics.title: Usability observation
details: Ask participants to accomplish a goal without naming the button or path you want them to use.
Consent, minimal data and accurate attribution matter; a self-walkthrough is useful but not independent user evidence.

topics.title: Experiment design
details: Name the unit assigned to a variant and the outcome before looking at results.
Operational canary routing, usability observation and randomized product experiments answer different questions.

reading.locator: Plan sessions, Design the tasks and Run a session: neutral goal-based tasks, a discussion guide, consistent instructions and honest observation.

assignment.title: An ethical hypothetical lineage-preview study
instructions: Write two neutral tasks for finding an input row and explaining why it was rejected; do not instruct the participant to click a named control.
Perform a clearly labelled self-walkthrough with synthetic data or document a genuinely consented optional peer review, without fabricating quotes.
Predeclare a hypothetical experiment comparing two presentations: assignment unit, outcome, safety guardrail and a result that would refute the hypothesis.
deliverables: A discussion/consent protocol and attributed observation note.
A falsifiable experiment brief with assignment and guardrails.
acceptanceCriteria: Tasks name user goals without revealing the intended interface path.
Any self-evaluation or hypothetical participant remains labelled as such.
The experiment defines its assignment unit and a credible reject/defer outcome before results.

questions.prompt: Which task is least leading for the proposed lineage preview?
choices: Click the blue Lineage button and read row 4
Find the source of this rejected row and explain the rejection
Confirm that the new panel is easy to use
questions.answer: Find the source of this rejected row and explain the rejection
questions.explanation: The task specifies the user goal without disclosing the desired interaction or inviting agreement. The other prompts teach the route or bias the evaluation.

questions.prompt: What limitation must accompany a solo self-walkthrough?
questions.answer: The evaluator already understands the intended design and is not an independent representative user. Report it as self-evaluation that can find obvious issues, not validated customer usability.
questions.explanation: Transparent attribution preserves the value of a bounded walkthrough without converting it into evidence from nonexistent participants.

reviewPrompts: Could the task wording explain an apparent success?
What result would make you reject the hypothesis?

modules.title: 05. Platform choices and experimental validity
modules.description: Evaluate API/platform alternatives and challenge the validity of attractive experiment results.

lessons.title: Choose an API product boundary and a reversible build-buy path
objectives: Compare build, reuse, buy and defer against a concrete workflow and constraints.
Include compatibility, ownership, migration and total cost in an API decision.

topics.title: Platform as a product
details: Start with one developer or operator journey and a supported contract, not a universal platform.
Ownership, error behavior, quotas and deprecation affect the experience as much as endpoint count.

topics.title: Build versus buy
details: Include integration, operation, switching and data-control costs rather than comparing only license prices.
Reversible experiments and exit criteria can reduce uncertainty without paid procurement or a production commitment.

reading.locator: What to consider when choosing technology, Understand the landscape and Allow for evolution; consider reversibility, total ownership cost and control of data.

assignment.title: A bounded data-recovery API decision
instructions: Compare implementing one local recovery endpoint, reusing a local command and deferring the feature for an explicitly hypothetical operator need.
Specify versioning, errors, idempotency, quota and ownership expectations; mark any unsupported reference capability as a learner extension.
Write a reversible proof-of-concept and an exit criterion; do not purchase, provision or send private data to a vendor.
deliverables: A bounded API contract and build/reuse/defer comparison.
An ownership/migration/exit decision record.
acceptanceCriteria: The comparison uses one defined workflow and credible alternatives.
Operational and switching costs are labelled assumptions, not invented bills.
The decision states compatibility, error and ownership obligations and a condition for changing course.

questions.prompt: Which consideration is missing from a comparison based only on license price?
choices: The product's logo color
A guarantee that newest is best
Integration, operation, switching cost and data control
questions.answer: Integration, operation, switching cost and data control
questions.explanation: The price of acquiring software is only one component of ownership. Integration and exit constraints can dominate the real decision even when a license is inexpensive.

questions.prompt: Why is 'add an endpoint' insufficient as a platform-product scope?
questions.answer: It omits the supported user journey, contract, ownership, error/permission behavior, compatibility and operational obligations. Those define whether the endpoint can be used safely and maintained.
questions.explanation: A platform product is a supported experience and responsibility boundary, not merely an implementation surface.

reviewPrompts: What makes the decision reversible?
Who owns the API after the prototype?

lessons.title: Diagnose invalid experiments before interpreting uplift
objectives: Identify sample-ratio mismatch, contamination and selection problems.
Distinguish absolute percentage-point changes, relative uplift and causal claims.

topics.title: Validity gates
details: A configured split can diverge from analyzed samples because of assignment, execution, logging or selection errors.
Diagnose sample-ratio mismatch before trusting effects; reweighting or dropping rows without a cause is not an automatic repair.

topics.title: Inference discipline
details: Predeclare analysis, stopping and multiple-comparison handling; repeated peeking or subgroup searching changes the false-positive problem.
A canary or before/after comparison does not establish random assignment, comparable populations or causal product impact.

reading.locator: How SRMs impact A/B tests, why they happen and diagnosis: trace assignment, execution, log processing and analysis before interpreting effects.

assignment.title: Audit a deliberately broken synthetic experiment
instructions: Start with a hypothetical 50/50 assignment of 1000 users but analyzed counts of 600 and 400; compute the Pearson two-cell discrepancy using expected counts of 500 each.
Compare conversion 20 of 200 versus 22 of 200: report the absolute percentage-point change and relative percentage change without claiming significance.
Create a fault tree for outcome-dependent logging, repeat users across variants, post-treatment filtering and repeated peeking; choose investigate/defer rather than inventing a corrected effect.
deliverables: A unit-labelled allocation/uplift calculation.
A validity fault tree and predeclared analysis/stop policy.
acceptanceCriteria: The allocation discrepancy is 40; it is not a p-value or a measured product effect.
Conversion changes from 10 to 11 percent: one percentage point absolute and 10 percent relative uplift.
The report withholds causal/ship claims until assignment, logging, selection and uncertainty are addressed.

questions.prompt: A synthetic test has unexplained sample-ratio mismatch and an attractive conversion estimate. What should happen first?
choices: Diagnose the mismatch and withhold the ship conclusion
Ignore it because uplift is positive
Remove inconvenient users until groups match
questions.answer: Diagnose the mismatch and withhold the ship conclusion
questions.explanation: SRM warns that the analyzed samples may not represent the intended randomized comparison. A positive estimate cannot repair assignment, logging or selection bias.

questions.prompt: Observed variant counts are 600 and 400; expected counts are 500 each. Sum each squared observed-minus-expected difference divided by its expected count.
questions.explanation: Each count differs from its expectation by 100. Each contribution is 10000 divided by 500, or 20; the sum is 40. This statistic is not itself a p-value.

questions.prompt: Explain why a synthetic canary route does not establish a randomized product experiment.
questions.answer: Routing may be deterministic or operationally selected, and the populations, exposure, outcomes and analysis may not meet experimental assumptions. Canary health evidence should not be converted into causal product uplift.
questions.explanation: Operational rollout safety and causal product inference are distinct questions. The design and data must support the particular claim being made.

reviewPrompts: Where could missing users have been selected by the outcome?
Are you reporting points, percent, a statistic or a p-value?

modules.title: 06. Unit economics, risk and delivery sequencing
modules.description: Connect financial units and accountable risk decisions to feasible technical delivery.

lessons.title: Calculate contribution and break-even without invented savings
objectives: Separate fixed cost, variable cost, revenue and contribution margin.
Explain break-even, relevant-range and uncertainty limits using consistent units.

topics.title: Unit economics
details: Contribution per unit is revenue less variable cost under a declared unit and accounting boundary.
Failure handling, support and operational work may be variable costs; ignoring them can make a comparison artificially attractive.

topics.title: Break-even and limits
details: Fixed cost divided by positive contribution gives break-even units under the stated linear assumptions.
Zero or negative contribution does not yield a finite nonnegative sales volume that covers positive fixed cost. Hypothetical prices are not actual revenue or savings.

reading.locator: CVP assumptions and Basics of the Break-Even Point: distinguish fixed/variable costs, contribution, relevant range and break-even in units versus revenue.

assignment.title: An original hypothetical service-economics model
instructions: Use an explicitly fictional service priced at 12 currency units per useful outcome, variable cost 8 per outcome and fixed cost 2400 per period.
Compute contribution and break-even units, then change variable cost to 12 and 13 and explain why naive division is not a viable break-even result.
Compare two local quality/cost options while including failed-request work and support assumptions; keep measured technical costs separate from hypothetical commercial prices.
deliverables: A unit-labelled base/sensitivity table.
A quality-cost recommendation with assumptions and missing business evidence.
acceptanceCriteria: Base contribution is 4 currency units per outcome and break-even is 600 outcomes per period.
Zero/negative contribution cases do not produce a claimed feasible break-even volume.
Prices, demand and financial effects remain explicitly hypothetical; no customer dollar savings are invented.

questions.prompt: Variable cost equals unit revenue while fixed cost is positive. Which conclusion is correct?
choices: Any sales volume immediately produces a profit
There is no finite break-even volume under this model
Break-even volume is zero
questions.answer: There is no finite break-even volume under this model
questions.explanation: Each additional unit contributes zero toward positive fixed cost. Dividing by zero is undefined; calling it zero-volume break-even reverses the economics.

questions.prompt: Unit revenue is 12, unit variable cost is 8 and period fixed cost is 2400 in the same currency. Enter break-even units for that period.
questions.explanation: Each unit contributes 4 toward fixed cost. Covering 2400 therefore requires 600 units; 2400 is a currency amount, not the requested unit count.

questions.prompt: Why does a cheaper inference request not necessarily reduce cost per useful outcome?
questions.answer: The cheaper configuration may fail more often, require retries/support or reduce quality. Count useful outcomes and all relevant work under the same workload before comparing the ratio.
questions.explanation: Optimizing one cost numerator while changing outcome quality or denominator can misrepresent the actual economic trade-off.

reviewPrompts: What is the unit being sold or delivered?
Which unmeasured cost could reverse your recommendation?

lessons.title: Sequence work around accountable risk and dependencies
objectives: Turn risk concerns into owned requirements and explicit acceptance evidence.
Choose a feasible delivery sequence including rollback and exception review.

topics.title: Risk requirements
details: Likelihood, impact, affected assets and uncertainty inform a risk decision; a generic 'secure' label does not close it.
Risk acceptance requires an accountable owner, scope, rationale and review condition rather than a blanket waiver.

topics.title: Delivery coordination
details: A dependency graph reveals blocked options and the consequences of delaying prerequisites.
Include privacy, support, incident handling and rollback owners rather than treating release as the end of responsibility.

reading.locator: Choosing technologies that support change, security risk management, data control and a map of dependencies; identify ownership and constraints before committing.

assignment.title: A recovery release with an explicit no-go risk
instructions: Create a hypothetical release plan for replayable data with contract checks, row lineage, operator preview and recovery documentation as separate work items.
Add dependencies and an explicit risk that output Parquet alone cannot reproduce accepted-run history; require source and successful-run journal retention.
Write an accept/mitigate/defer decision with owners, evidence needed, rollback and an exception-review trigger; do not claim legal compliance from the exercise.
deliverables: A dependency graph and acceptance ownership table.
A scoped risk/exception/rollback decision.
acceptanceCriteria: The plan cannot schedule a dependent release before its safety prerequisite.
Every accepted exception has an owner, rationale, scope and review trigger.
The decision preserves actual recovery dependencies and distinguishes learning review from legal/security certification.

questions.prompt: A release exception has no owner or review condition. What is the appropriate response?
choices: Treat it as permanent approval
Hide it from the roadmap
Keep it unresolved until accountable acceptance or mitigation is defined
questions.answer: Keep it unresolved until accountable acceptance or mitigation is defined
questions.explanation: An exception is a continuing decision with consequences. Without ownership and review conditions it becomes an unbounded waiver rather than a controlled risk choice.

questions.prompt: Explain why recovery documentation may be a release dependency rather than optional post-launch polish.
questions.answer: If operators cannot identify required source/journal artifacts or safely restore them, a failure can leave the service unrecoverable. The release decision must account for that operational requirement.
questions.explanation: Delivery includes the ability to operate and recover the system. A successful happy-path demo does not satisfy that responsibility.

reviewPrompts: Which dependency is a safety requirement rather than a preference?
Who can accept the remaining risk and when must it be revisited?

modules.title: 07. Launch decisions and stakeholder responsibility
modules.description: Make explicit go/defer/rollback decisions and communicate disagreements without inventing organizational experience.

lessons.title: Predeclare launch, stop and rollback criteria
objectives: Define release criteria against actual observable signals and supported rollback behavior.
Distinguish operational rollout evidence from long-term reliability or causal impact.

topics.title: Release decisions
details: A criterion names the population, window, threshold, owner and action, not just 'monitor closely'.
A missing signal is an unknown, not a passing guardrail. Rollback itself needs a tested compatible path.

topics.title: Canary limitations
details: A small rollout can reveal certain failures without proving long-term production availability.
Operational routing and a healthy canary do not establish random assignment or product outcome causality.

reading.locator: Release Engineering Principles and Balancing Release Velocity and Reliability: reproducible artifacts, small changes, measured canary behavior and rollback decisions.

assignment.title: A synthetic release go/defer record
instructions: Define a hypothetical release window with 200 eligible requests and a no-go threshold above 1 percent failed requests; include ownership and a missing-signal rule.
Evaluate a fixture with three failed requests and a separate fixture with absent telemetry.
Describe a tested or explicitly proposed rollback path and explain what this local window cannot prove about production reliability or customer benefit.
deliverables: A release decision table with thresholds and actions.
A rollback/missing-signal review and limitation statement.
acceptanceCriteria: Three failures among 200 eligible requests is 1.5 percent and triggers the stated no-go rule.
Absent telemetry is not treated as a successful guardrail.
Implemented versus proposed rollback and local versus production evidence are clearly separated.

questions.prompt: The required failure-rate telemetry is absent during a release window. How should that guardrail be reported?
choices: Unknown; follow the predeclared missing-signal action
Passed because no failures were observed
Passed because the page still loads
questions.answer: Unknown; follow the predeclared missing-signal action
questions.explanation: Missing observations do not establish an absence of failures. A defensible release process defines how missing evidence changes the decision.

questions.prompt: Why cannot a short local canary establish a monthly production SLO?
questions.answer: Its duration, environment, workload and failure exposure differ from the monthly production population. It can test bounded behavior but cannot establish that longer reliability claim.
questions.explanation: An operational observation must retain its measurement boundary; extrapolating it into a production guarantee discards the relevant uncertainty.

reviewPrompts: What happens if a signal disappears?
Can rollback restore compatible state as well as code?

lessons.title: Negotiate a decision with explicit trade-offs and ownership
objectives: Present a disagreement fairly and separate evidence from preference.
Assign decision rights, operational responsibility and conditions for revision.

topics.title: Stakeholder reasoning
details: Technical, commercial, support and risk perspectives can optimize different outcomes.
Describe dissent accurately rather than inventing stakeholder quotes or implying actual PM employment.

topics.title: Accountable strategy
details: An outcome strategy connects target users, a choice, expected mechanism and evidence needed.
A decision record names alternatives, ownership, unresolved risk and what would change the choice.

reading.locator: Develop roadmaps collaboratively around outcomes and review them as evidence changes; explain both what is selected and what is not being done.

assignment.title: A hypothetical commerce scope negotiation
instructions: Create an explicitly hypothetical disagreement: product wants partial refunds, engineering supports full refunds only, and operations needs reliable reconciliation.
Write a balanced decision record covering build, defer and narrower release, using actual reference limits and clearly hypothetical demand/cost assumptions.
Assign a decision owner, incident responsibility and a revision trigger; write separate short explanations for technical and nontechnical audiences.
deliverables: A decision record with alternatives and accurately attributed assumptions.
Two audience-specific explanations and an ownership/revisit table.
acceptanceCriteria: Partial refunds are not presented as implemented merely because stakeholders want them.
Each alternative has a genuine disadvantage and dissent is represented fairly.
Ownership and a concrete revision condition are explicit; no real negotiations or commercial outcomes are invented.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical stakeholder prefers a feature outside the implemented scope. Which response preserves accountability?
choices: Describe it as delivered to maintain enthusiasm
State the gap and compare a narrower release, implementation or deferral
Claim unanimous agreement without discussion
questions.answer: State the gap and compare a narrower release, implementation or deferral
questions.explanation: A decision record must retain the difference between preference and capability. Honest alternatives allow stakeholders to choose with awareness of cost, risk and missing work.

questions.prompt: What makes a revision trigger more useful than 'revisit later'?
questions.answer: It identifies a specific observation, risk change, capability or evidence threshold and an owner responsible for reassessing the decision.
questions.explanation: A concrete trigger converts an indefinite promise into a reviewable decision process without pretending future outcomes are already known.

reviewPrompts: Can the dissenting perspective recognize itself in your summary?
What evidence would change the chosen scope?

modules.title: 08. Post-launch learning and an honest three-project defense
modules.description: Revise product decisions from reproducible evidence and defend the boundaries of a complete educational case study.

lessons.title: Revise a roadmap without converting correlation into impact
objectives: Analyze a synthetic post-launch-style dataset with stable metric definitions.
Revise a roadmap while retaining negative results, changed populations and uncertainty.

topics.title: Post-launch interpretation
details: Before/after populations may differ in composition, exposure or instrumentation.
A percentage-point change describes arithmetic, not proof that a release caused it.

topics.title: Learning loops
details: Keep the original hypothesis and decision record rather than rewriting the goal after seeing results.
Negative or inconclusive evidence can justify deferral, instrumentation repair or a changed priority.

reading.locator: Combine measurement with research and iterate from both; define consistent purpose, hypotheses, population and data sources before interpreting a trend.

assignment.title: A reproducible synthetic roadmap review
instructions: Analyze a synthetic before cohort with 8 successes among 80 eligible users and an after cohort with 12 among 100; retain raw counts and metric definitions.
Compute rates and absolute percentage-point change using a local script or SQL, then add a population-mix or logging-change counterexample.
Revise two roadmap priorities using the uncertainty and at least one negative result, without claiming that a release caused the observed change.
deliverables: A reproducible cohort analysis and counterexample.
A revised roadmap linked to the original hypothesis and contrary evidence.
acceptanceCriteria: The rates are 10 and 12 percent and the absolute change is two percentage points.
The write-up distinguishes descriptive change from causal impact and identifies a credible confounder.
The revised roadmap retains negative/inconclusive results rather than rewriting them as success.

questions.prompt: A before/after metric improved while population mix also changed. What is justified?
choices: The release definitely caused the improvement
The outcome proves customer adoption doubled
Report the descriptive change and investigate the changed population
questions.answer: Report the descriptive change and investigate the changed population
questions.explanation: A simultaneous composition change offers another explanation for the metric. Descriptive arithmetic remains valid, but a causal release claim needs a suitable design and evidence.

questions.prompt: The rate changes from 8/80 to 12/100. Enter the absolute change in percentage points, not relative percent.
questions.explanation: The before rate is 10 percent and the after rate is 12 percent. Their absolute difference is two percentage points; the relative increase would instead be 20 percent.

questions.prompt: Give an evidence-based reason to prioritize instrumentation repair over a new feature after launch.
questions.answer: If changed logging or missing eligible users prevents valid outcome measurement, repairing that instrumentation may be necessary before comparing alternatives or claiming an improvement.
questions.explanation: Learning depends on valid evidence. A feature roadmap that ignores a broken measurement boundary can optimize misleading signals rather than user outcomes.

reviewPrompts: Did the population or metric definition change?
Which negative result changed your next decision?

lessons.title: Defend three technical product cases without inflated claims
objectives: Integrate discovery, requirements, measurement, economics and release decisions across three canonical projects.
Separate implemented reference behavior, hypothetical product assumptions and independent learner evidence.

topics.title: Case-study integrity
details: The commerce, retrieval and replayable-data cases are the same shared projects used by other profiles, not relabelled extra applications.
Raw private source, receipts, personal resumes, employer data and participant information do not belong in public learning artifacts.

topics.title: Professional defense
details: Defend a rejected alternative, a negative result and a remaining capability gap for each case.
Professional Practice is a learning level; an AI-assisted implementation or self-report is not certification, job readiness or independent mastery.

reading.locator: Roadmap objectives, shared understanding and evidence-driven revision; connect the three case decisions to actual constraints and clearly hypothetical outcome assumptions.

assignment.title: One integrated three-project decision dossier
instructions: Use the canonical commerce workflow, retrieval evaluation and replayable data projects; create one original hypothetical product case per project rather than inventing extra apps.
For each, connect a problem/segment hypothesis, bounded PRD, requirement evidence, instrumentation/analysis, economics assumptions and release/defer decision.
Personally explain a working behavior, make and test a bounded change, diagnose a failure and defend the remaining risks using local synthetic artifacts.

Record which claims are actual learner observations, reviewed reference capabilities, unreviewed/absent features or hypothetical product assumptions; do not copy private code or receipts into the tracker repository.
deliverables: Three clearly hypothetical problem/segment/PRD case briefs with canonical project identities.
A requirement and capability coverage matrix including missing work.
Executable local synthetic instrumentation/analysis and unit-labelled economics.
A three-case release/roadmap decision dossier with rejected alternatives and negative results.
An independent learner explanation/change/debug/test record kept private.
acceptanceCriteria: Exactly the three canonical PM project intents are used; shared projects are not counted as different applications.
Each PRD requirement has specific evidence or an explicit unimplemented/unknown label.
Synthetic personas, experiments, prices and outcomes are never described as real interviews, customers, adoption or revenue.
Every numerical statement is traceable to original input data, a reproducible calculation and its units.
Each case includes an adverse result, a credible rejected alternative and a justified release/defer decision.
Private source, receipts, resume data, employer/client information and secrets are absent from public artifacts.
The learner's own explanation, modification, diagnosis and tests are distinct from an agent-built reference or existing completion record.

questions.prompt: A reference project is tested and available, but the learner has not explained or changed it. Which readiness claim is honest?
choices: Reference available; independent learner readiness not yet demonstrated
Learner professionally certified
All learner gates completed automatically
questions.answer: Reference available; independent learner readiness not yet demonstrated
questions.explanation: Implementation availability and individual competence are different evidence categories. Tests run by an agent or another reviewer do not demonstrate the learner's own understanding or ability to modify the system.

questions.prompt: How should a case study present a desired feature whose reference review is still pending?
questions.answer: Describe it as a learning target or unverified reference capability, avoid an implemented claim, and name the evidence needed. Any learner-built extension must be labelled and independently demonstrated.
questions.explanation: A pending review is an explicit uncertainty, not permission to infer capability from a project name or intended scope.

reviewPrompts: Which claim would you remove if challenged for evidence?
Can you reproduce and explain one failure without relying on an agent's receipt?

sources.title: GOV.UK Service Manual: user research
sources.notes: Methods and public-service examples, not a requirement to publish research or collect personal data.

sources.title: Microsoft Research: experimental validity
sources.notes: SRM diagnosis and limitations; original exercises do not copy experimental datasets.

sources.title: OpenStax: managerial accounting
sources.notes: Contribution and break-even concepts, linked rather than rehosted.

sources.title: Google SRE: canary releases
sources.notes: Operational release guidance, not proof of randomized product impact.

limitations: Professional Practice is a learning stage, not a professional certification, employment claim, salary promise or independently verified mastery.

All required case studies use original synthetic data and explicitly hypothetical personas, discovery, experiments and economics. Never invent real users, interviews, adoption, revenue or causal impact.
Private GitHub references require authorized access; the tracker cannot grant it. No private source, raw receipts, personal resumes, employer/client material or secrets may be published.
Reference implementation availability, original build evidence and the learner's independent readiness remain separate; none automatically completes the others.
Core study is free and local. Videos are not fabricated: these new lessons are honestly reading-led, and the existing PDF inventory is unchanged.
Government, research and accounting sources provide contextual methods. They do not establish jurisdiction-specific legal compliance, professional assurance or current commercial facts.
Actual interviews, market validation, pricing in a real business and organizational leadership require real experience and evidence beyond these hypothetical learning cases.
